also: do you have room for us?

terms.gloss: Do you have a table free?
terms.grammar: dative of the possessor with est; vacuus, -a, -um, free, not taken
terms.comment: A sentence of ours: we have found no set phrase for asking for a table in the authors searched (Plautus, Terence, Petronius, Cicero’s letters, Martial) or in Traupman, Morgan–Owens, or Levi–Bini. It is built from vacuus of a place not taken (see “free”) and the dative of the possessor, which is how Latin says “do you have”. Say how many you are first, as a separate sentence: Duo sumus., Quattuor sumus.. The nearest the comedies come is Epignomus’s sī superfiat locus, “if there were room to spare” (Plaut. Stich. 592).

phrases.latin: Duo sumus: estne vōbīs mēnsa vacua?
phrases.english: A table for two, please: do you have one free?

phrases.latin: Quattuor sumus, duo adultī et duo puerī.
phrases.english: There are four of us, two adults and two children.

phrases.latin: Edepol tē vocem lubenter, sī superfiat locus.
phrases.english: I’d gladly invite you, by Pollux, if there were any room to spare.

phrases.latin: Age accumbe igitur. cedo aquam manibus, puere, appōne hīc mēnsulam.
phrases.english: Come, take your place, then. Water for my hands, boy; set a little table here.

phrases.latin: Trēs sumus: estne vōbīs mēnsa vacua?
phrases.english: There are three of us: do you have a table free?
